title: Oct 2020 (Set 1)
subtitle: Verified Answer Key (100/100 Qs) + Crisp Simple-English Explanations

items.title: Q1 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: Inductive method differs from deductive method in drawing its conclusion from
items.explanation: Induction moves from particular instances to a general conclusion. Deduction moves from general truths to particular cases.

items.title: Q2 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: Which of the following information has now been excluded while making an entry for a book in the 8th edition of MLA Handbook for Writers of Research Papers?
items.explanation: The MLA 8th edition dropped the place of publication from book entries, except in special cases.

items.title: Q3 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: Which of the following journals deals with the analysis of only theoretical concepts?
items.explanation: boundary 2 is a journal of theory and criticism. Granta is a literary magazine, Manoa a regional literary journal and Arethusa a classics journal.

items.title: Q4 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Roman Jakobson
items.stem: Which one of the following statements by Roman Jakobson is true about metaphor and metonymy?
options: Metaphor is alien to the continuity disorder whereas metonymy is alien to similarity disorder
Metaphor is alien to the similarity disorder and metonymy to the continuity disorder
Metaphor is alien to both similarity disorder and continuity disorder and metonymy is common to both
Metaphor is common to both similarity disorder and continuity disorder but metonymy is alien to both
items.explanation: In Jakobson's aphasia study, patients with a similarity disorder cannot produce metaphor, and patients with a contiguity disorder cannot produce metonymy.

items.title: Q5 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Mikhail Bakhtin
items.stem: Who among the following theorists defines novel as “a phenomenon multiform in style and variform in speech and voice”?
items.explanation: Mikhail Bakhtin describes the novel as 'multiform in style and variform in speech and voice' in his essays on heteroglossia.

items.title: Q6 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Stanley Fish
items.stem: Who among the following critics is said to have developed the notion of ‘interpretive communities’?
items.explanation: Stanley Fish introduced 'interpretive communities' in Is There a Text in This Class? (1980).

items.title: Q7 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Metaphor differs from simile in that
options: A comparison in metaphor is usually explicit whereas in simile it is implicit
A comparison in metaphor is usually implicit whereas in simile it is explicit
Neither metaphor nor simile is rooted in comparison
Simile involves superimposition while metaphor involves comparison
items.explanation: A simile states the comparison openly using 'like' or 'as'. A metaphor implies it without such words.

items.title: Q8 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Plato
items.stem: The two broad divisions of reality in Plato’s theory of reality are:
items.explanation: In the Republic's divided line, Plato splits reality into the visible world and the intelligible world.

items.title: Q9 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Horace
items.stem: Who among the following called the ‘Poetasters’, “The rhyming friends”?
items.explanation: Horace mocked second-rate versifiers (poetasters) in his Satires and Epistles.

items.title: Q10 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Philip Sidney
items.stem: Who among the following refutes Plato’s charge that poets are liars, by arguing that the poet “nothing affirms, and therefore never lieth”?
items.explanation: In An Apology for Poetry, Sidney says the poet 'nothing affirms, and therefore never lieth'.

items.title: Q11 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Alexander Baumgarten
items.stem: Who among the following coined the term, ‘aesthetics’?
items.explanation: Alexander Baumgarten coined 'aesthetics' in the 1730s and 1750s from the Greek word for perception.

items.title: Q12 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Benedict Anderson
items.stem: Who among the following drew attention to the role of print languages in enabling the rise and spread of nationalism?
items.explanation: Benedict Anderson argued in Imagined Communities that print capitalism and print languages created national consciousness.

items.title: Q13 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Theodor Adorno, Max Horkheimer
items.stem: Which one of the following captures accurately the view of Frankfurt School of Critical Theory?
options: the culture industries instil in their mass audiences a capacity to question and transform
The culture industries engender passivity and conformity among their mass audiences
Power and culture are two distinct modes of social articulation, separate from each other
The analysis of culture should be divorced from politics and power relations
items.explanation: Adorno and Horkheimer argued that the culture industry makes audiences passive and conformist.

items.title: Q14 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Stuart Hall
items.stem: Which of the following groups of words correctly states the stages of communication as envisioned by Stuart Hall in his essay “Encoding, Decoding”?
items.explanation: Hall's circuit has production, circulation, distribution/consumption and reproduction.

items.title: Q15 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India · Charles Grant
items.stem: Who among the following held that “the people of Hindustan” are “a race of men lamentably degenerate and base, retaining but a feeble sense of moral obligation...”?
items.explanation: Charles Grant wrote this in his Observations on the State of Society among the Asiatic Subjects of Great Britain (1792), arguing for English education.

items.title: Q16 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem: Which agency among the following made a distinction between the teaching of English as a skill and the teaching of English literature?
items.explanation: The Kothari Education Commission (1964–66) separated English as a language skill from English literature.

items.title: Q17 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem: Which agency among the following was of the view that “use of English divides the people into two nations, the few who govern and the many who are governed”?
options: The Working Group (UGC) on Regional Languages (1978)
items.explanation: This view is usually credited to the Kothari Education Commission (1964–66).

items.title: Q18 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India · Ernest Gowers
items.stem: Who is the author of The Complete Plain Words?
items.explanation: Sir Ernest Gowers wrote The Complete Plain Words (1954), a guide to clear official English.

items.title: Q19 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India · Deborah Tannen
items.stem: Who among the following has coined the term, ‘genderlect’?
items.explanation: Deborah Tannen introduced 'genderlect' in You Just Don't Understand (1990) for differing male and female speech styles.

items.title: Q20 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem: “Nice day again, isn’t it?” This sentence is an example of:
items.explanation: Small talk like this keeps social contact going and carries no real information, which is phatic communication.

items.title: Q21 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem: Language allows us to talk about the things and events not present in immediate environment. Which of the following terms describes this property of language?
items.explanation: Displacement is the ability to talk about things that are absent in time or place.

items.title: Q22 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Francis Bacon
items.stem: In “Advancement of Learning” Francis Bacon divides poetry into three divisions :
items.explanation: Bacon divides poetry into narrative, representative (dramatic) and allusive (parabolic).

items.title: Q23 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Ezra Pound
items.stem: Which one of these essays by Ezra Pound defines an Image as “that which presents an intellectual and emotional complex in an instant of time”?
items.explanation: The definition of the Image is in Pound's essay 'A Retrospect' (1918, from 'A Few Don'ts').

items.title: Q24 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit VI: English in India · Nissim Ezekiel, V.S. Naipaul
items.stem: Who wrote the essay “Naipaul’s India and Mine” (1984) as a reply to V.S. Naipaul’s An Area of Darkness?
items.explanation: Nissim Ezekiel wrote 'Naipaul's India and Mine' in reply to Naipaul's travel book.

items.title: Q25 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Jorge Luis Borges, Robert Burton
items.stem: Which of the following short stories by Jorge Luis Borges has its epigraph from The Anatomy of Melancholy?
items.explanation: 'The Library of Babel' opens with an epigraph from Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy about the twenty-three letters.

items.title: Q26 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Fyodor Dostoevsky
items.stem: How does Christ respond to the Grand Inquisitor’s accusations in Brothers Karamazov?
options: He kneels before the Grand Inquisitor
He kisses the Grand Inquisitor on his lips
He begins to weep in remorse
He says, “Mea culpa, mea culpa, mea maxima culpa”
items.explanation: Christ says nothing and gently kisses the old Inquisitor on his lips. The Inquisitor then lets him go.

items.title: Q27 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: In which short story does the narrator witness a consumptive young man named Mr. Shaynor recreate “The Eve of St. Agnes” in a trance?
items.explanation: In Kipling's 'Wireless', the chemist's assistant Mr. Shaynor, in a trance, writes lines like Keats's 'The Eve of St. Agnes'.

items.title: Q28 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem: Mr. Pumblechook is a character in:
items.explanation: Mr. Pumblechook is Pip's pompous uncle in Dickens's Great Expectations.

items.title: Q29 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charlotte Brontë
items.stem: To which of these boarding schools is Jane Eyre sent by her aunt Mrs. Reed?
items.explanation: Mrs. Reed sends Jane to Lowood Institution, a charity school.

items.title: Q30 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Edgar Allan Poe
items.stem: Which of the following short stories by Edgar Allan Poe has a narrator who has a rival with the same name and uncanny physical resemblance?
options: “The System of Doctor Tarr and Professor Fether”
items.explanation: In 'William Wilson' the narrator is haunted by a double with the same name and look.

items.title: Q31 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Robert Browning
items.stem: What does the titular Setebos in Robert Browning’s “Caliban upon Setebos” refer to?
options: The original name of Sycorax, Caliban’s mother
The brutal god in whom Caliban believes
The name of the island in which Caliban lives
The monster whom Caliban is afraid of
items.explanation: Setebos is the cruel god Caliban imagines ruling the world, taken from The Tempest.

items.title: Q32 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Philip Larkin
items.stem: Which of the following poems by Philip Larkin ends with the line “Never such innocence again”?
items.explanation: 'MCMXIV' ends with 'Never such innocence again'. It looks back at 1914 before the First World War.

items.title: Q33 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Edmund Spenser
items.stem: Which of the following is true in relation to Edmund Spenser’s Faerie Queene?
options: A letter addressed to Sir Walter Raleigh was prefixed to the 1590 edition of the poem
A letter addressed to Sir Walter Raleigh was appended to the 1590 edition of the poem
A letter addressed to Sir Walter Raleigh was prefixed to the 1596 edition of the poem
A letter addressed to Sir Walter Raleigh was appended to the 1596 edition of the poem
items.explanation: Spenser's 'Letter to Raleigh', explaining the poem's plan, was printed at the end of the 1590 edition.

items.title: Q34 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · John Milton
items.stem: Who was Milton’s model when he recast the first edition (1667) of Paradise Lost in 10 books to 12 books of the second edition (1674)?
items.explanation: Milton re-divided the poem into twelve books to match Virgil's Aeneid.

items.title: Q35 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Harold Pinter
items.stem: In Harold Pinter’s play The Birthday Party, who suggests the idea of having a birthday party?
items.explanation: Goldberg takes up Meg's mention of Stanley's birthday and proposes the party.

items.title: Q36 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem: Which of the following characters instruct Faustus in the dark arts?
items.explanation: Valdes and Cornelius, two friends skilled in magic, teach Faustus necromancy in Marlowe's play.

items.title: Q37 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Samuel Beckett
items.stem: What is the content of the suitcases that Lucky carries in the second Act of Waiting for Godot?
items.explanation: In Act 2, Lucky still carries the bag, which Pozzo says holds sand.

items.title: Q38 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · William Congreve
items.stem: In which Act of William Congreve’s The Way of the World does the Proviso scene between Mirabell and Millamant take place?
items.explanation: The famous proviso scene, where the lovers set terms for marriage, is in Act IV.

items.title: Q39 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · William Shakespeare
items.stem: Which of the following statements is correct in relation to Shakespeare’s works?
options: The Folio edition appeared in the sixteenth century and the ‘quartos’ appeared in the seventeenth century
The ‘quartos’ appeared during his lifetime and the Folio edition appeared posthumously
The Folio edition appeared during his lifetime and the ‘quartos’ appeared posthumously
The ‘quartos’ refer to works written between 1594 and 1599, and the Folio includes works written between 1608 and 1613
items.explanation: Many quartos were printed in Shakespeare's lifetime, and the First Folio came out in 1623, seven years after his death.

items.title: Q40 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: Who is the author of the short play, The Dark Lady of the Sonnets?
items.explanation: George Bernard Shaw wrote The Dark Lady of the Sonnets (1910).

items.title: Q41 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem:
Which two of the following citations conform to the documentation format of the eighth edition of the MLA Handbook?
(A) Baron, Naomi S. “Redefining Reading: The impact of Digital Communication Media”. PMLA, vol 128,no.1, Jan.2013,PP. 193-200.
(B) Adichie, Chimamanda Ngosi. “On Monday of Last Week”, The Thing Around Your Neck. London: Knopf, 2009. 74-94
(C) Baron, Naomi S. “Redefining Reading: The impact of Digital communication Media”. PMLA 128.1 (2013): 193-200.
(D) Adichie, Chimamanda Ngosi. “On Monday of Last Week”. The Thing Around Your Neck, Alfred A. Knopf, 2009, PP. 74-94.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: MLA 8 uses vol., no., date and pp. for articles (A), and publisher and pp. without the city for books (D). (B) and (C) follow older formats.

items.title: Q42 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem:
While assembling a working bibliography which two of the following reference sources will be particularly useful to a literary researcher?
(A) MLA International Bibliography
(B) New Princeton Encyclopaedia of Poetry and Poetics
(C) Library of Congress Catalogue
(D) Reader’s Guide to Periodical Literature
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: The MLA International Bibliography and the New Princeton Encyclopaedia are standard literary research tools.

items.title: Q43 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem:
Which two of the following periodicals are devoted to feminist theoretical discussion?
(A) Spectrum
(B) Signs
(C) Chrysalis
(D) Transition
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Signs and Chrysalis are feminist journals. Spectrum and Transition are not.

items.title: Q44 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Roland Barthes
items.stem:
Which two of the following features shall apply to Roland Barthes’s notion of a ‘writerly text’?
(A) In case of writerly text, the reader accepts the meaning without too much reading effort
(B) A writerly text tends to focus attention on what is written
(C) A writerly text makes the reader a producer
(D) A writerly text tends to be self-conscious.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In S/Z a writerly text makes the reader a producer of meaning, and it is self-conscious about its own writing. A readerly text is the one read passively.

items.title: Q45 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Jacques Derrida
items.stem:
A deconstructive reading of a text shows that
(A) a text is to be read always in a context
(B) there is nothing except the text
(C) a text may betray itself
(D) a text may possess an ascertainable meaning
(E) there is an endless postponement of meaning
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Deconstruction holds that 'there is nothing outside the text', that a text can undercut itself, and that meaning is endlessly deferred.

items.title: Q46 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Cherríe Moraga, Gloria Anzaldúa
items.stem:
Which two of the following edited the defining work of third-wave feminism, This Bridge Called My Back: Writings by Radical Women of Color?
(A) Audre Lorde
(B) Barbara Smith
(C) Gloria Anzaldua
(D) Cherrie Moraga
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: This Bridge Called My Back (1981) was edited by Cherríe Moraga and Gloria Anzaldúa.

items.title: Q47 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · P.B. Shelley, Philip Sidney
items.stem:
Which two of the following poets defended poetry against Plato’s denigration of Poetry?
(A) John Dryden
(B) P.B. Shelley
(C) T.S. Eliot
(D) Philip Sidney
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Sidney's An Apology for Poetry and Shelley's A Defence of Poetry are the classic replies to Plato.

items.title: Q48 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Samuel Johnson
items.stem:
Which two of the following are Samuel Johnson’s statements about metaphysical poets?
(A) they were singular in their thoughts
(B) they were careful in their diction
(C) they effected combination of dissimilar images
(D) they avoided occult resemblances
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: In the Life of Cowley, Johnson says the metaphysicals were singular in thought and yoked together dissimilar images. He says they discovered, not avoided, occult resemblances.

items.title: Q49 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · T.S. Eliot
items.stem:
Which two of the following plays are mentioned in T.S. Eliot’s “Tradition and Individual Talent”?
(A) Agamemnon
(B) Antigone
(C) Othello
(D) Dr. Faustus
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Eliot refers to the Agamemnon and to Othello in the essay.

items.title: Q50 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Laura Mulvey, Stuart Hall
items.stem:
Which two of the following essays have proved particularly productive in the disciplinary practices of Cultural Studies?
(A) Laura Mulvey, “Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema”
(B) Viktor Shklovsky, “Art as Technique”
(C) Sigmund Freud, “The Uncanny”
(D) Stuart Hall, “Encoding/decoding”
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Mulvey's essay on the male gaze and Hall's encoding/decoding model have been central to Cultural Studies.

items.title: Q51 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem:
Which of these following statements are true about Pidgin and Creole?
(A) Pidgin begins as Creole and eventually becomes the first language of a speech community
(B) Creole begins as Pidgin and eventually becomes the first language of a speech community
(C) Pidgin is simple but a rule governed language developed for communication whereas Creole is free from grammatical rules
(D) Pidgin and Creole evolve successively out of a situation where speakers of mutually unintelligible languages develop a shared language for communication (often based on one of those languages)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: A creole grows out of a pidgin once children learn it as a first language. Both arise when speakers of different languages need a shared tongue.

items.title: Q52 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem:
Which two of the following words are borrowed into English from Czech?
(A) pistol
(B) robot
(C) sauna
(D) coach
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: 'Pistol' (from Czech pišťala) and 'robot' (from Czech robota) came into English from Czech. Sauna is Finnish and coach is Hungarian.

items.title: Q53 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem:
Which two of the following meanings are admissible for the following sentences :
“You do not know how good oysters taste”
(A) You do not know that oysters taste good as food
(B) You do not know how the oysters taste when cooked
(C) You do not know what the oysters taste when they eat
(D) You do not know how the good oysters taste when they eat
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: The sentence can mean that oysters taste good (A) or that good oysters taste a certain way (D).

items.title: Q54 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift) · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Daniel Defoe
items.stem:
Which two of the following works are Daniel Defoe’s historical narratives?
(A) History of the Rebellion
(B) Meditations on a Broomstick
(C) A Journal of the Plague Year
(D) Memoirs of a Cavalier
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Defoe wrote A Journal of the Plague Year and Memoirs of a Cavalier. History of the Rebellion is Clarendon's and Meditations on a Broomstick is Swift's.

items.title: Q55 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Peter Ackroyd
items.stem:
Which two of the following are non-fictional works by Peter Ackroyd?
(A) Escape from Earth
(B) The Great Fire of London
(C) The English Ghost
(D) English Music
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Escape from Earth and The English Ghost are non-fiction. The Great Fire of London and English Music are novels.

items.title: Q56 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Darwin, Charles Dickens
items.stem:
Which two of the following were published in the year 1859?
(A) On the Origin of Species
(B) A Tale of Two Cities
(C) Alice in Wonderland
(D) Silas Marner
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Darwin's On the Origin of Species and Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities appeared in 1859. Alice came in 1865 and Silas Marner in 1861.

items.title: Q57 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.stem:
In his “Self-Reliance” which two qualities does Emerson refer to as “the Chancellors of God”?
(A) Truth
(B) Cause
(C) Spirit
(D) Effect
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Emerson writes that 'Cause and Effect are the Chancellors of God'.

items.title: Q58 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Virginia Woolf
items.stem:
Which two of the following are part of Virginia Woolf’s collection of autobiographical essays?
(A) “A Will to Word It”
(B) “A Sketch of the Past”
(C) “A Faint Hue of the Past”
(D) “Am I a Snob”
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Moments of Being includes 'A Sketch of the Past' and 'Am I a Snob?'. The other two titles are invented.

items.title: Q59 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Paul Auster
items.stem:
Which two of the following novels are part of Paul Auster’s New York Trilogy?
(A) The Book of Illusions
(B) Ghosts
(C) The Locked Room
(D) Winter Journal
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: The New York Trilogy is City of Glass, Ghosts and The Locked Room.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is correct but Statement II is false
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Cultures differ across the world, so Statement I is false. Cultures overlap and mix, so exclusive blocs cannot be drawn, and Statement II is true.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
items.explanation: Because cultural forms sit where cultural networks intersect, their meaning cannot be tied to one culture alone, so R explains A.

items.title: Q91 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)

items.stem:
Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow:
WHEN I’M ALONE
‘When I’m alone’ the words tripped off his tongue
As though to be alone were nothing strange
‘When I was young’, he said, ‘when I was young...’
I thought of age, and loneliness, and change,
I thought how strange we grow when we’re alone,
And how unlike the selves that meet, and talk,
And blow the candles out, and say good-night,
Alone ...The word is life endured and known.
It is the stillness where our spirits walk
And all but in most faith is overthrown.
—Siegfried Sassoon

options: The normal fate of a human being all his life
The normal fate of a human being when he is young
Not unlike being with others whom we meet
Not strange as a person should feel alone
items.explanation: The old man says 'When I'm alone' casually, 'as though to be alone were nothing strange'. Marked doubtful because the option wording is awkward.

items.title: Q94 · Oct 2020 (Set 1)

items.stem:

Poetry, as a mania – one of Plato’s two higher forms of “divine” mania – has, in all its species, a mere insanity incidental to it, the “defect of its quality”, into which it may lapse in its moment of weakness; and the insanity which follows a vivid poetic anthropomorphism like that of Rossetti may be noted here and there in his work, in a forced and almost grotesque materialising of abstractions, as Dante also became at times a mere subject of the scholastic realism of the Middle Age.
— Walter Pater

In the above passage poetry is described as one of Plato’s two higher forms of ‘divine’ madness. Which is the other one?
Choose the correct option?
items.explanation: In the Phaedrus Plato names poetic, prophetic, ritual and erotic (love) madness as divine. Love is the other one named here.

—A Midsummer Night’s Dream

Who was in love with Demetrius?
items.explanation: Helena loves Demetrius, though he is promised to Hermia and loves her at first.

items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem:
Read the following and then answer the questions that follow
He went to work in this preparatory lesson, not unlike Morgiana in the Forty Thieves: looking into all the vessels ranged before him, one after another, to see what they contained. Say, good M’Choakumchild. When from thy boiling store, thou shalt fill each jar brim full by-and-by, dost thou think that thou wilt always kill outright the robber Fancy lurking within – or sometimes only maim him and distort him.
—Dickens, Hard Times

In the expression “... looking into all the vessels ranged before him...”, which one of the following devices is used?
items.explanation: The children are described as vessels to be filled, which is a metaphor, since no 'like' or 'as' is used.
